Mr. Speaker, the motion proposed by the hon. member for Welland suggests action which would be of benefit to all classes of workers. It would not be the be-all and end-all which we might expect from full legislation, but I think it would bring about the immediate remedial benefit which is needed at the present time. I realize that the parliamentary secretary has said that the government is aware of this problem; but as the hon. member for Timmins pointed out, if it is aware of the problem then possibly it will accept this motion and implement it so that some immediate action can be taken to help our workers in Canada. They are the ones who are most maligned in respect of the portability of pensions and the vesting rights of employees.
During this past year we have had some incidents of this problem in my riding. English Electric Company of Canada closed its St. Catharines plant and over 300 heads of families were left without employment. Many of these people are still unemployed, and the prime reason given by many industries in the area for not employing some of these people was that they were too old to fit into their pension plans. The companies could not take a chance with those who sought employment and felt that company pension plans could not be extended to them. The Foster-Wheeler plant closed their processing division, and the same thing happened with them. Many of these people were skilled employees who had put in anywhere from 15 to 18 years with the company. All they were able to get from the funds they had put in to provide for their security in retirement years was the exact amount of money they had contributed. In endeavouring to seek new employment they were at a loss, even though they were specialists in their type of work. Very few companies wished to hire them because of their age and their inability to fit in with company pension plans. The Canadian National Railways at St. Catharines terminated its bus transportation franchise in 1960 and all their employees endeavoured by all legal means to have the pension funds which they had built up transferred to the municipality of St. Catharines so that they could continue with some possibility of security in their retirement years. This was not possible and they had to become employees of the city of St. Catharines transit commission and start all

over again. Despite the number of years these people had worked for the C.N.R., they will not be able to provide adequately for their retirement years. This means for example that their families will not be provided with proper educational benefits. As the hon. member for Timmins pointed out, this motion is not intended to cover all the factors, but it will provide the government with a chance to show that it really is aware of the problem facing workers today, and of the need for portability of pensions.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. F. Jones (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every one of the speakers in this debate has testified to the importance of this resolution, and I certainly agree with them. This is a most important resolution, and we must look carefully at it. I want to say how much I appreciate the interest in this question shown by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan). However, I point out that he stated explicitly during the course of his remarks that portable pensions are a matter for provincial governments. This is clearly set out in the British North America Act under section 92 which relates to property and civil rights. Old age pensions generally, so far as they might be affected by this matter, are provided for in section 94. I do not think I need refer further to it, except to point out that there is perhaps an analogy here. Section 94A says:
It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions.
I submit that those provisions were put into the B.N.A. Act because there was a clear recognition of the fact that matters such as pensions-all pensions-are within the field of provincial jurisdiction. They are a matter to be decided by the provinces. The recognition of this problem is clearly demonstrated in the speech from the throne presented by this government to this parliament. I refer to page 9 of Hansard, where the speech from the throne states:
As pension plans have become ever more widely extended in Canadian business, it has been increasingly recognized that measures are essential to protect the interests of those affected and in particular to ensure that the benefits earned are portable when workers move from job to job.
Then I would underline this sentence.
Provincial legislation would be required for this purpose in most cases-
That is in all cases except those which come specifically under federal jurisdiction.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
Would the hon. member mind if I finished my quotation? The speech from the throne continues:
-and several provinces are considering proposals of this nature. My government will be prepared to place before you complementary legislation to deal with industries under federal jurisdiction when adequate progress has been made by provinces.
The point has been stated, indeed admitted, by the hon. member for Welland-and it is clearly demonstrated by the citations I have given-that portable pensions are a matter for the provinces. They are a matter of provincial rights. The hon. member for Welland said that this resolution is to help bring about or force portability of pensions in the provinces. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is an attempt to do indirectly what the parliament of Canada cannot do directly. It is an attempt to subvert the constitution.
Can you imagine the situation, Mr. Speaker, if we were to agree to a resolution such as this whereby the federal government could use taxing measures to force the people in the provinces to disobey provincial laws? If we were to use taxing measures in order to force the people in the provinces to act in conformity with federal thinking, whether those actions were matters relating to the provinces under the constitution or whether they were matters relating to the possibilities of the federal government, this would be a clear invasion of provincial rights. It is an insidious sort of invasion and I am sure the hon. member for Welland did not intend that. As the course of this debate develops, I am sure my friend the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) who is an expert on constitutional matters, and my friend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), who is highly qualified in this regard, may develop further this particular point. However, I would draw it to the attention of the house that it would be most unfortunate if this business of portable pensions were to become muddied up and involved in a conflict between the provinces and the federal government. This is something which I think all hon. members would wish to avoid. It has been the course of the Conservative government to try to advance the cause of portable pensions.
References were made to this matter earlier, I think a year or so ago, in his budget by the then minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice. Again, it is referred to in the speech from the throne of this year. Always the emphasis has been on co-operation with the provinces in order to bring about the objective of portability which eventually will 27507-3-165
Portability of Pensions bring about so much good to the people of this country. The matter of portable pensions is something of which I think we can say all hon. members in all parts of the house are in favour. A few moments ago the hon. member for Vancouver East wished to ask a question. I must apologize to him for asking his permission to finish that portion of my remarks before accepting it. Perhaps he might ask the question now, if he so desires.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Saskatoon for his consideration, Mr. Chairman. I am wondering whether the hon. member has actually read the resolution. If so, would he not see that this resolution with respect to the Income Tax Act is asking for a regulation which was in effect up until 1957 or 1958, as I recall it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
No. The resolution here is quite a different thing from the one mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay East. What the resolution says is this-and I will quote it right now so that he may have the advantage of studying it with us while we are discussing this particular point. The resolution states as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of encouraging reasonable early vesting of pension rights of employees-
How?
-by disallowing in whole or in part the employer's claims for a reduction of the expenses of pensions for income tax purposes where reasonable vesting provisions are not adopted.
In others words, this is an invasion of the rights of the provinces by the federal government through the back door of the Income Tax Act. This is the point I am making. This is the thing we must avoid. We must avoid the invasion of provincial rights. I think all hon. members in this house will join with me when they come to realize the danger there is in this sort of resolution, particularly all those who are sincerely interested in advancing the cause of portable pensions.
It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to go much further into this particular matter. However, I wished to point out some of the problems which have been raised incidentally by the hon. member for Welland who, I am sure, enjoys the respect of all members of the House of Commons. However, he gets led into a situation and it is a rather dictatorial one. He said that a bill based on this resolution would not allow a workman to get his hands on his pension money. Although he said that, I am sure he could not possibly have meant it. I do not think this house or any other legislature should dictate to workmen what they shall do with their own

Portability of Pensions money. That is their business. Any relationships they may be able to work out with their employers over pensions is a matter of business, too.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what I said was "get his hands on his pension money early", as he does now if he quits after two or three years. I did not mean that he would never get his hands on his pension money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
This is the point. I would think that one of the rights which all people assert is the right to do with their own what they wish to do, so long as it does not hurt somebody else. Therefore, if in their wisdom they decide they wish to get their hands on their pension money, that is their decision, unless they enter into some sort of arrangement with the employer which by agreement, either individually or through their unions, precludes them from doing this. Surely it is fundamental, Mr. Chairman, that we should not start legislating in order to force things down other people's throats if they themselves do not want them. To take such a course is the essence of the over protective socialist state. We have already had so many examples in so many parts of the world of the stultifying effect of this state paternalism that I am sure the hon. member for Welland, on reflection, would wish to avoid that course.
I know there are many others who wish to enter into this debate. I will therefore close my remarks at this stage, hoping that the hon. members who follow me will be able to deal further and more extensively than I have done with this particular problem of the invasion of provincial rights.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext: My point is only a question. The hon. member who has just taken his seat indicated that he did not wish to accept a question during his major remarks. However, I thought the important part of his remarks was that in which he suggested that responsibility for portability of pensions related to provincial jurisdiction. As he was the first speaker representing the government after the resolution was introduced by my friend the hon. member for Welland, may I ask him this question. What would his remarks be with respect to the portability of pensions either interprovincially or internationally?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that there are a number of incidental and quite unimportant assumptions here. One was that I was the first government speaker following the mover of this resolution. Of course, that is not so. However, that has nothing to do with the point at issue. The question of whether pensions are portable internationally takes us no further at all on this question of


unconstitutionality. Once you establish pensions on a basis of agreement with the provinces so that the constitution is not infringed, it can then become a question of relationship between the governments involved in passing enabling legislation to deal with international portability of pensions. This matter does not pose a major problem at all. The problem we face at the moment with regard to the question of the portability of pensions is that of getting rapport between the provinces and the federal government on the best means to follow in obtaining portability of pensions, by combining their legislative powers and by passing enabling legislation, as has been suggested in the speech from the throne and on other occasions by ministers of this government.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to compliment the hon. member for Welland for his tenacity in bringing this matter forward again. I know that for quite a number of years, going back I think, as far as 1956, the hon. member together with myself and other members raised this question in the interests of those receiving pensions not on a contributory basis. The history of this matter goes back as far as 1953 when the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers first took it up in a serious way in an endeavour to make industrial pensions more portable. They were frustrated in their efforts to negotiate, particularly because the large industries maintained that with respect to non-contributory pension plans the employee had no claim on the pension until he reached retirement age.
That union went into the matter quite thoroughly and unearthed the government blue book containing regulations with respect to income tax. They found that there was a regulation in the blue book which, among other things, provided that in order for a pension plan to be accepted by the income tax authorities certain vesting rights should rest with the employee. I might say that this regulation was not enforced in the case of non-contributory pension plans.
The union pressed its case year after year with the assistance of the hon. member for Welland and other members in the house and some industries finally recognized the force of their argument. I know this is true in the case of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. Up to that time they had refused adamantly even to discuss the matter of vesting any rights of employees in their pension plan which, as I have said, was noncontributory. Following a great deal of negotiation and pressure by the union officials, although they actually had no authority to discuss the matter, the company finally saw that this was a very justifiable request and

Business of the House
in June of 1958 the bylaws of the pension plan were amended to provide that an employee who had served for 20 years and had reached the age of 50 would have his rights preserved in the plan. As I have said, this was a move that was made under pressure from people such as the hon. member for Welland and others.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext: And the government.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member says "and the government". I have not been informed of any great action on the part of the government. I inquired why this change came about so suddenly and I found that there was no action on the part of the government. As a matter of fact, the present government withdrew the blue book from circulation. The hon. member cannot take any credit for the government whatsoever. It was the pressure exerted by the union and by members in the opposition who brought this matter forward from time to time. While I agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones) that this is not the answer, it is something that the federal government can and did do for years and could have continued to do on the basis of their authority to make regulations under the Income Tax Act. This is not an invasion of provincial rights. Let us not have any of that small talk.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Welland, people age, become ill and for various reasons need to leave their employment. Certainly it is only right that they should have a vesting interest in their pension plan. What has happened so far is the thin edge of the wedge and something has been accomplished. Let us give the hon. member for Welland full credit for what he has done in the past and let us vote on this motion now and pass it.

subtopic: PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we were going to vote on this motion I am afraid I would find myself unable to vote in favour of it. On reading the resolution the first thought that occurred to my mind was that the Income Tax Act can be used as a quite powerful weapon. The suggestion here is that the weapon of disallowing pension contributions in whole or in part as an expense item be used if there is not reasonably early vesting of the pension rights of employees. This sounds to me like pushing somebody pretty hard, and I wonder whether the hon. member who moved the motion has really considered what he is doing here. The resolution is broad enough to cover contributory pension plans where the union and
the employer have come together and have made an agreement between them as to when the pension plan will vest. As a result there is vesting according to their agreemnt.
The resolution suggests that the federal government will have to set up a body which would be responsible for deciding when pensions should vest, and what schemes they thought were suitable and werer regarded by them as vesting early enough. The government point of view would then be imposed on those companies in substitution for the point of view agreed on by the employer and the employees.
I am afraid there is not time to go into many of the considerations that an employer has to take into account when he is setting up a plan to cover people who are going to be working for a long time. There are many good and pressing reasons why he wants to encourage the employee as much as possible to stay a long time with the company. Six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
